clue.text: Gambler calls for a stiff drink with gold leaves

parts.note: a double is a twice-sized measure of spirits
or is the heraldic word for gold
quits means leaves, as in quits the room

explanation.surface: A gambler orders a strong drink, then walks out with his golden winnings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' just joins the drink and the gold to the last piece; the answer is the gambler's call to stake everything on one more bet.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is what a betting player says when offering to risk all winnings again on one throw.

clue.text: One up, old man? Maybe this will make you forget

definitions.text: One up, old man? Maybe this will make you forget

parts.words: One up, old man? Maybe this will make you forget
parts.note: the opening asks a friend whether he is high, and the rest describes a drug taken for oblivion

explanation.surface: Someone checks whether a friend is on a high and offers something to blot out memories.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the poppy drug: being 'up' is being high, and its old reputation was as a bringer of forgetfulness.
explanation.definitionFit: The narcotic from poppies was famed for dulling memory and sending users into dreamy forgetfulness.

clue.text: Hue that is becoming to a guide

parts.note: brown is a colour, a hue
i.e. abbreviates id est, that is

explanation.surface: A colour is said to suit a girl guide well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'becoming to' looks like praise of the colour but simply links the pieces to the definition. A Brownie is a member of the junior branch of the Girl Guides.
explanation.definitionFit: The junior section of the Girl Guide movement has members named after a household sprite, so each is a young guide.

clue.text: Farewell his life's ambition?

parts.note: farewell read as two words, fare well, means to eat and drink finely, the lifelong aim of a gourmet

explanation.surface: Someone bids goodbye to the dream he has chased all his life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Farewell' looks like goodbye; split it into 'fare well' and it is the aim of a devotee of fine food and drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of pleasure in good food and wine makes dining handsomely the goal of living.

clue.text: What's left of the priest in religion

indicators.note: in places the priest's name within the letters for the religion

parts.note: RC stands for Roman Catholic, a religion
Eli is the priest of Shiloh in the Book of Samuel

explanation.surface: A remnant of the clergyman lingers on within the faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What's left' reads as part of the surface but is the definition: a remnant or keepsake of the past.
explanation.definitionFit: A surviving fragment or keepsake from the past is what remains after the rest is gone.

clue.text: To suffer is certainly not to overcome

explanation.surface: Enduring hardship is said to be the very opposite of triumphing over it.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the answer into 'under' and 'go', the exact opposite of 'over' and 'come'.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear or experience something is to suffer it, and going under is the reverse of coming over.

clue.text: Buffer wrapper material

explanation.surface: A protective layer of packaging cloth is described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buffer' looks like padding, but a buffer is a naval petty officer, and the answer is old slang for a sailor as well as waterproof canvas.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarred canvas covers cargo, and the same word was slang for a seaman, of whom a naval buffer is one.

clue.text: The old girl's a sound and distinguished campanologist

indicators.note: the clue says the bell-ringing dame is a sound, so we hear her and take the spelling of the old word

parts.note: a dame is a woman honoured with a title, so a bell dame would be such a woman ringing bells

explanation.surface: An elderly lady is praised as a fine and eminent bell-ringer.
explanation.walkthrough: A campanologist rings bells; a titled bell-ringing woman would be a 'bell dame', which said out loud gives the archaic word for an old woman.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word for an aged woman, often a hag, means an old girl.

clue.text: Greeting in Coronation Street that's always good for a laugh

definitions.text: that's always good for a laugh

explanation.surface: A hello on a TV soap street is offered as a reliable source of laughs.
explanation.walkthrough: Coronation Street is a long-running British TV soap; its gossip Ena Sharples would be greeted 'Hi, Ena', which runs together into the animal famed for its laughing call.
explanation.definitionFit: The African scavenger called the laughing kind has a cry like cackling, and greeting Ena runs to the same letters.

clue.text: This we once found in our leader

definitions.text: This we once found in our leader

parts.words: This we once found in our leader
parts.note: a leader is a newspaper's leading article, where writers once used the royal 'we' in an unsigned piece of opinion

explanation.surface: Someone recalls discovering this quality in the person heading their group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader' suggests a chief, but here it is a newspaper's leading article, written in the impersonal 'we'.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's opinion column is called its leader, and its writers speak as 'we'.

clue.text: Classic bowler

explanation.surface: A traditional cricketer, or a timeless style, is suggested.
explanation.walkthrough: The Classics are five big British flat horse races, one of them run at Epsom; a bowler is a hard round felt hat, called by the same name in America.
explanation.definitionFit: The Epsom race is one of the five Classics, and a round felt hat bears the same name across the Atlantic.

clue.text: The spirit that followed the Q.E.

explanation.surface: A ghost trailed behind the great ocean liner Queen Elizabeth.
explanation.walkthrough: Q.E. looks like the liner Queen Elizabeth, but it is 'quod erat', and the Latin tag continues 'demonstrandum', whose opening five letters are an evil spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: A malign supernatural being is a spirit, and the same letters begin the Latin word after quod erat.

clue.text: O Woman! Make up your mind!

definitions.text: O Woman! Make up your mind!

parts.words: O Woman! Make up your mind!
parts.note: Walter Scott's Marmion begins a famous couplet O Woman! in our hours of ease, and the next word describes her as unable to decide

explanation.surface: An exasperated man begs a dithering woman to come to a decision.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening words are a quotation from Scott's poem Marmion, whose next line calls woman 'coy, and hard to please' after the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott calls woman undecided and fickle, the condition the plea to decide complains of.

clue.text: Kipling's cat was kind of cross

explanation.surface: An author's pet cat was in a bad temper.
explanation.walkthrough: Kipling's story 'The Maltese Cat' is about a polo pony, not a feline; 'cross' is the noun, the eight-pointed cross of the Knights of Malta.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling titled a polo-pony story after an island-named cat, and the Knights of Malta gave their name to a cross.

clue.text: As the invention of a vital cure may doubtless be

definitions.text: As the invention of a vital cure may doubtless be

indicators.note: an invention is something made up, so the letters of the phrase are made up into a new word

explanation.surface: Discovering a life-saving remedy would surely make a fortune for its inventor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'invention of' shuffles VITAL CURE; read as a whole, the clue says a new medicine would be profitable.
explanation.definitionFit: A money-spinning thing is profitable, as a patent on a new remedy would surely be.

clue.text: Song of the Goblin

explanation.surface: A tune sung by a mischievous little creature.
explanation.walkthrough: As a verb the answer means to sing heartily; as a noun it is a Scandinavian cave-dwelling giant or goblin.
explanation.definitionFit: To sing in a rolling, cheerful way is one sense, and a mythical Norse monster is the other.

clue.text: Food includes variety of a sort on board

definitions.note: board is an old word for table, so the phrase stands for a thing set out on the breakfast table

indicators.note: the food word takes the other letters within it

parts.note: tack is food, as in hardtack ship's biscuit

indicators.note: a variety is a different arrangement, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Food comes with a varied selection of some kind on a platter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variety of' turns A SORT into OASTR, and 'includes' puts it inside TACK. 'board' here is a dining table, as in bed and board.
explanation.definitionFit: A holder for slices of grilled bread is a fixture of the breakfast table, an old sense of board.

clue.text: Crafty request by a game loser

definitions.text: Crafty request by a game loser

parts.words: Crafty request by a game loser
parts.note: a beaten player asks cunningly for a return match in the hope of getting even

explanation.surface: A sly appeal comes from someone who has just lost a match.
explanation.walkthrough: A beaten player asks to be given a chance to get his own back, a return game.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting even after a defeat is retaliation, and a loser asks for a chance at it in a return game.

clue.text: Many a wine holder in the main room

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, many
a bin is a rack or store for bottles of wine

explanation.surface: Plenty of wine racks are kept in the principal room of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the main' is not the chief room but the sea, so the definition is a room on a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A compartment for sleeping aboard ship is a room at sea, the main being an old word for the ocean.

clue.text: Sent unceremoniously off on a package tour?

explanation.surface: Someone is hustled out of the house and onto a cheap holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'package tour' looks like a holiday; read it as a parcel being wrapped up, done up in a bundle.
explanation.definitionFit: Hustled off rudely is the first sense; tied up as a parcel is the second.

clue.text: Perhaps money order to a friend in need of recognition

definitions.text: order to a friend in need of recognition

explanation.surface: Possibly a postal remittance is sent to a pal who wants to be noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'money order' looks like a postal payment; split it. The sentry's challenge was 'Advance, friend, and be recognised'.
explanation.definitionFit: A loan paid ahead of time is money of this kind, and a sentry orders an approaching friend to step forward.

clue.text: One's surrounded by vessels of the city state

indicators.note: the numeral sits within the two containers

parts.note: a vat is a large vessel for liquids
a can is a metal vessel
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A single person finds himself hemmed in by the ships of a city state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vessels' looks like ships, but here gives two containers, VAT and CAN, with I placed between them.
explanation.definitionFit: The papal enclave in Rome is the world's smallest sovereign city state.

clue.text: Angle a cut to point

definitions.note: a noun standing for the adjective that describes an angle under ninety degrees

parts.note: E is east, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Someone trims something on a slant to give it a sharp tip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'point' looks like sharpening, but it is a compass point, E. The definition stands for an angle smaller than a right angle.
explanation.definitionFit: An angle less than ninety degrees is the sharp kind, so the word names such an angle.

clue.text: Anti-rigging device

parts.note: rigging suggests fixing an election, but it is a sailing ship's ropes and masts, which linked cannonballs were fired to tear down

explanation.surface: A gadget for stopping a ballot or race from being fixed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rigging' suggests cheating; it is the ropes of a sailing ship, which naval gunners shredded with two balls joined by a length of chain.
explanation.definitionFit: Two cannonballs joined by a chain were fired to cut a ship's masts and ropes.

clue.text: Post it quickly

parts.note: post-... means with great speed, so the word that follows post in that phrase is 'it' and means quickly

explanation.surface: Someone is told to mail a letter without delay.
explanation.walkthrough: The old phrase 'post-haste' means very fast; the answer is the word that goes after 'post', and it means speed.
explanation.definitionFit: Speed or hurry is what follows post in the phrase meaning very swiftly.

clue.text: A metaphor from the tightrope

indicators.note: from tells us to take the letters out of the word that follows it

explanation.surface: A figure of speech is borrowed from the circus wire-walker's act.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits in the last five letters of 'tightrope'.
explanation.definitionFit: A figure of speech is a general term, and a metaphor is one example of it.

clue.text: Hunter whose dog has his days

definitions.text: Hunter whose dog has his days

parts.words: Hunter whose dog has his days
parts.note: the constellation of the giant huntsman is followed by Sirius, the Dog Star, whose rising marks the dog days of summer

explanation.surface: A hunter keeps a hound that is having its moment of glory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'every dog has his day' is a proverb, but the dog days are the hot weeks when Sirius, the hunter's dog star, rises with the sun.
explanation.definitionFit: The giant hunter of Greek myth is a constellation, attended by the Dog Star Sirius.

clue.text: Is this balance connected with the scales of justice?

definitions.text: Is this balance connected with the scales of justice?

parts.words: Is this balance connected with the scales of justice?
parts.note: accounting's preliminary balance shares its first word with a court hearing, the business of justice

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a kind of balance has to do with justice's scales.
explanation.walkthrough: A bookkeeper's preliminary balance of accounts goes under the same word as a court case, hence the link to justice.
explanation.definitionFit: A court hearing goes before justice, and a bookkeeper's first check of accounts carries the same word.

clue.text: Looking for change, Sir?

parts.note: someone politely asks a gentleman patting his pockets whether he is hunting for coins

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper asks a customer if he is after some small coins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' might hint at an anagram of 'Sir'; it is coins, and the gentleman is rummaging for them.
explanation.definitionFit: Rummaging for coins is hunting for them, which the word for an active hunt describes.

clue.text: By no means a quick calculation of course

definitions.text: By no means a quick calculation of course

parts.words: By no means a quick calculation of course
parts.note: quick is the old word for alive, so its opposite is lifeless; a calculation of course is a navigator's working out of a ship's position

explanation.surface: Something is said to be naturally anything but a speedy sum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' looks like 'naturally' but is a ship's course; 'quick' is the old sense of living, as in 'the quick and the dead'.
explanation.definitionFit: Navigators reckon a ship's position from speed, heading and time elapsed, without stars or landmarks.
